entities.summary:
Simon of Tournai was a pivotal scholastic philosopher and theologian active at the nascent University of Paris in the late twelfth century, whose career, concluding with his death around 1201, encapsulates the intellectual ferment of the High Middle Ages. He stood at the forefront of integrating Aristotelian logic and metaphysics into Christian theology, a process that profoundly shaped the curriculum and methodology of the burgeoning university system. His work contributed significantly to the development of systematic theology, influencing the intellectual landscape that would define the golden age of scholasticism.

Simon's primary contribution stemmed from his lectures and disputations in Paris, where he rigorously applied Aristotelian principles to complex theological questions. He is widely associated with the *Summa theologica*, also known as *Institutiones in sacram paginam*, a foundational early scholastic work that aimed to systematize Christian doctrine, preceding and laying groundwork for monumental syntheses by figures like Alexander of Hales and Thomas Aquinas. His teaching, characterized by its intellectual daring, reportedly included propositions that challenged orthodox beliefs, such as the controversial claim that 'the three laws [of Moses, Christ, and Muhammad] are all fables,' leading to accusations of heresy and illustrating the volatile intellectual climate.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Simon of Tournai holds significant regional and thematic importance as an early master at the University of Paris, whose systematic theological work and engagement with Aristotle directly influenced the development of scholasticism and the intellectual trajectory of 13th-century European thought.
